short: Selling a whole business unit as one package for a single lump-sum price, without putting separate prices on each asset and liability.
kid: Imagine selling your whole lemonade stand, with the table, jug and cups, for one price. You do not sell each cup on its own, just the stand as one bundle.
detail: A slump sale is the transfer of one or more undertakings, meaning a running business with its assets, liabilities, staff and contracts, for a lump-sum consideration with no value assigned to individual items. The selling company keeps its legal identity and receives the payment under a business transfer agreement. Indian tax law treats the undertaking as a single capital asset: the gain is the price minus the net worth of the undertaking, and it is long-term if the undertaking was held for more than 36 months (section 50B of the Income-tax Act, 1961, under the rules as of 2025). Companies use slump sales to sell a division or move it into a subsidiary without a tribunal process. Do not confuse it with an itemised asset sale, where each asset is priced separately, or with a demerger, where shareholders, not the company, receive shares of the new entity.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells its packaging division to XYZ Ltd for ₹500 crore on a slump sale basis. The division's net worth (assets of ₹420 crore minus liabilities of ₹100 crore) is ₹320 crore, so ABC records a capital gain of ₹500 crore − ₹320 crore = ₹180 crore.
formula: Capital gain on slump sale = Sale consideration − Net worth of the undertaking

short: A tribunal- or court-approved plan to merge, demerge or restructure companies, binding all shareholders and creditors once the required majorities vote for it.
kid: Imagine the whole class has to agree on a new plan for sharing the toy box. If most children vote yes and the teacher approves, everyone follows the new plan, even those who said no.
detail: A scheme of arrangement is a statutory route for mergers, demergers, share swaps, capital reductions and debt restructurings. In India it runs under sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013: each class of shareholders and creditors must approve it by a majority in number representing three-fourths in value of those voting, and the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) must then sanction it. Listed companies first need a no-objection letter from the stock exchanges, which consult SEBI. Once sanctioned, the scheme binds dissenting holders too, its big advantage over buying shares one by one. A composite scheme bundles several steps, say a demerger plus a merger, into one document. Expect 8 to 12 months or more. The UK uses similar schemes for takeovers. A common confusion is to think a simple majority of shares is enough; both the headcount and value tests apply.
example: When HDFC Ltd merged into HDFC Bank through a composite scheme that took effect on 1 July 2023, shareholders received 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC shares. An investor holding 100 HDFC shares therefore got 100 × 42 / 25 = 168 HDFC Bank shares.

short: Part of an acquisition price that the buyer pays later only if the acquired business hits agreed targets, such as revenue or profit.
kid: You buy a friend's lemonade stand for some coins now. If it sells lots of lemonade next summer, you give your friend a few extra coins, just as you both agreed.
detail: An earn-out makes part of the purchase price depend on the target's performance after closing, typically measured on revenue, EBITDA or product milestones over one to three years. It bridges a valuation gap: the seller believes in strong growth, while the buyer wants proof before paying for it. Earn-outs are common in founder-led, startup and pharma deals. Under Ind AS 103 and IFRS 3, the buyer records the expected earn-out at fair value on the acquisition date, and later changes in that estimate usually flow through profit and loss. The big practical risk is disputes, because the buyer now runs the business and controls the costs that drive the metric. In cross-border Indian share deals, FEMA rules as of 2025 allow only up to 25% of the price to be deferred, within 18 months. Do not confuse an earn-out with deferred consideration, a fixed amount paid later whatever the performance.
example: Say XYZ Ltd buys ABC Ltd for ₹200 crore upfront plus an earn-out of ₹50 crore payable if ABC's year-two EBITDA exceeds ₹40 crore. If ABC reports ₹45 crore, the seller gets the full ₹250 crore, of which the earn-out is 20%; if ABC reports ₹35 crore, the price stays at ₹200 crore.
formula: Total consideration = Upfront payment + Earn-out payments actually earned

short: A strategy that buys a takeover target's shares after a deal announcement to earn the gap between its market price and the offer price.
kid: A friend promises to buy your toy car for 10 sweets next week. Today someone sells you the car for 9 sweets, because they worry the friend might change their mind. If the friend keeps the promise, you end up 1 sweet ahead.
detail: After a takeover is announced, the target usually trades a little below the offer price. That gap, the deal spread, exists because the deal may fail on regulatory, financing or shareholder grounds, and because money is tied up until closing. Merger arbitrageurs buy the target and, in stock-for-stock deals, short the acquirer in the exchange ratio so that only the spread remains. Returns are small and steady when deals close, but a broken deal can wipe out many deals' worth of gains in a day as the target falls back, which is why the strategy is also called risk arbitrage. Hedge funds dominate it globally; in India, a version appears around open offers and delisting offers. Do not confuse it with riskless arbitrage: a wide spread is the market's signal that it doubts the deal will close.
example: Say XYZ Inc. agrees to buy ABC Inc. for $50 a share in cash and ABC trades at $48. The spread is $2 / $48 = 4.17%; if the deal closes in six months that is roughly 8.3% a year, but if it collapses and ABC falls back to $38, the arbitrageur loses $10 a share.
formula: Deal spread = (Offer price − Target's current price) / Target's current price

short: The first time a private company sells shares to the public and lists them on a stock exchange, so anyone can trade them.
kid: Your lemonade stand belonged to just your family. Now you invite the whole street to buy tiny pieces of it, and they can swap those pieces with each other later.
detail: An IPO is when a company first offers shares to public investors and lists on an exchange such as NSE or BSE. It can include a fresh issue, where new shares raise money for the company, and an offer for sale, where existing holders such as founders or private equity funds sell their stake. In India the process runs under SEBI's ICDR Regulations: bankers draft a DRHP, SEBI reviews it, the company files an RHP and a price band, anchor investors bid a day early, the issue stays open for at least three working days, and shares list on the third working day after closing under the rules as of 2025. Listing brings capital, liquidity and visibility, but also disclosure duties and quarterly scrutiny. The common confusion is assuming IPO money always goes to the company; in an offer for sale it goes to the sellers.
example: Say ABC Ltd's ₹1,000 crore IPO is a ₹400 crore fresh issue plus a ₹600 crore offer for sale; only ₹400 crore reaches the company. A real case: Hyundai Motor India's October 2024 IPO of about ₹27,870 crore was entirely an offer for sale by its Korean parent, so the Indian company itself raised nothing.
formula: IPO size = Fresh issue + Offer for sale

short: A public sale of new shares by a company that is already listed, to raise more money after its IPO.
kid: Your lemonade stand already shares pieces with the street. Later you need a bigger jug, so you offer the street a few more pieces to pay for it.
detail: A follow-on public offer is a public share sale by a company that is already listed. In India, an FPO usually means a further issue of new shares to the public under SEBI's ICDR Regulations, with a price band, book building and retail participation much like an IPO. New shares dilute existing holders but bring fresh money to the company. Globally, a follow-on offering may instead be a secondary offering, where existing shareholders sell and the company receives nothing, so check which kind it is. Indian FPOs are rare because a QIP or rights issue is quicker and cheaper; notable ones include Yes Bank's ₹15,000 crore FPO in 2020 and Vodafone Idea's ₹18,000 crore FPO in 2024. Since the shares already trade, FPOs are usually priced at a discount to the market price, and the FPO abbreviation should not be confused with farmer producer organisations in Indian news.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 100 crore shares and sells 20 crore new shares at ₹50 in an FPO, raising ₹1,000 crore. An investor who owned 1 crore shares (1%) now owns 1 crore out of 120 crore, or about 0.83%.
formula: Post-issue ownership = Shares held / (Existing shares + New shares issued)

short: A quick way for a listed Indian company to raise money by selling new shares only to institutions such as mutual funds and insurers.
kid: Your lemonade stand needs coins fast. Instead of asking the whole street, you ask only a few big grown-ups who know a lot about lemonade stands, and they decide quickly.
detail: A QIP lets a listed Indian company issue equity shares, or securities convertible into them, only to qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) such as mutual funds, insurers, banks and foreign portfolio investors. It runs under Chapter VI of SEBI's ICDR Regulations and needs a shareholders' special resolution but no pre-filing with SEBI, so a deal can be launched and closed within days using a placement document. Under the rules as of 2025, the floor price is the average of the weekly high and low closing prices over the two weeks before the relevant date, a discount of up to 5% is allowed, at least 10% of the issue is offered to mutual funds, and no single allottee may take more than 50%. Banks and NBFCs use QIPs heavily. Do not confuse a QIP with a preferential allotment, which goes to named investors under different pricing and lock-in rules.
example: Say ABC Ltd's QIP floor price works out to ₹400 and the board uses the 5% discount, pricing shares at ₹380. To raise ₹1,900 crore it issues ₹1,900 crore / ₹380 = 5 crore new shares to institutions.
formula: Shares issued = Amount raised / Issue price, where Issue price ≥ Floor price × (1 − Permitted discount)

short: A share offer where the company announces one exact price in advance, and investors simply apply for shares at that price.
kid: You put a sign on your lemonade stand: one cup costs two coins. Everyone pays the same, and you only find out at the end of the day how many cups people wanted.
detail: In a fixed price issue the issuer and its lead manager set a single price in the offer document before the issue opens, and investors apply for a number of shares at that price. Demand is known only when the issue closes, and the price does not move even if the offer is heavily oversubscribed. This was the standard Indian method before book building was introduced in the mid-1990s. Most mainboard IPOs are now book built, but many SME IPOs still use a fixed price. Under SEBI rules as of 2025, at least half of the net offer in a fixed price issue goes to retail individual investors. The trade-off: it is simple and transparent for small investors, but the issuer may leave money on the table by pricing too low, or face undersubscription by pricing too high. Do not confuse it with the cut-off price option in book-built issues.
example: Say ABC Ltd offers 50 lakh shares at a fixed ₹100, a ₹50 crore issue. Applications arrive for 1.5 crore shares, so the issue is 1.5 crore / 50 lakh = 3 times subscribed, yet the price stays at ₹100 and shares are allotted proportionately or by lottery.
formula: Issue size = Fixed price × Number of shares offered

short: A way of pricing a share offer by collecting investors' bids at different prices within a range, then setting the final price from that demand.
kid: Before baking cookies, you ask friends how many they want and what they would pay. Then you pick a fair price from everyone's answers and bake the right amount.
detail: Book building is the price-discovery method used for most IPOs and large share sales. The company and its book running lead managers announce a price band, and investors bid for a quantity of shares at chosen prices inside it. The bankers compile these bids into an order book showing how much demand exists at each price. The final issue price is set where demand comfortably covers the shares offered, often at the top of the band when the book is oversubscribed. In India, retail investors can bid at the cut-off price, agreeing to pay whatever final price is set, and institutional appetite is visible early through the anchor book. Abroad, bankers also weigh the quality of investors, not just volume, and allocate shares at their discretion. The common confusion is thinking each investor pays their own bid price; everyone in a category pays the same final price.
example: Say ABC Ltd offers 1 crore shares with a price band of ₹190 to ₹200. At ₹200 investors bid for 1.4 crore shares, so the book is 1.4 times covered even at the top, and the bankers price the issue at ₹200, raising 1 crore × ₹200 = ₹200 crore.

hl: upper end of the price band
lower end of the price band
top end of the price band
short: The range between the lowest and highest price at which investors may bid for shares in a book-built offer such as an IPO.
kid: You tell friends a cookie will cost between 4 and 5 coins. They say how many they want at each price, and then you choose the final price.
detail: In a book-built issue the company and its lead managers fix a price band: a floor price, the minimum bid, and a cap price, the maximum. Investors bid within it, and the final issue price is set from the demand book, often at the cap when the issue is well oversubscribed. Under SEBI rules as of 2025, the cap may be at most 120% of the floor and must be at least 105% of it, and the band must be announced at least two working days before the issue opens. Together with the lot size, the band sets the minimum application amount for retail investors. A tight band signals confidence about valuation; a wide one shows uncertainty. Do not confuse an IPO price band with the daily price bands, or circuit limits, that exchanges set on how far a listed share may move in one day.
example: Say ABC Ltd sets a price band of ₹475 to ₹500, so the cap is ₹500 / ₹475 = 105.3% of the floor, within the rules. With a lot of 30 shares, a retail investor bidding at the cap pays 30 × ₹500 = ₹15,000 per lot.
formula: Minimum application amount = Lot size × Cap price

short: A large institutional investor that commits to buy shares in an IPO before it opens to the public, signalling confidence to other investors.
kid: Before the lemonade stand opens, a well-known grown-up buys the first big jug. Other people see that and feel safer buying too.
detail: Anchor investors are qualified institutional buyers, such as mutual funds, insurers and foreign funds, who are allotted shares one working day before an IPO opens. In India, under SEBI rules as of 2025, a company can allot up to 60% of the QIB portion to anchors, each anchor must apply for at least ₹10 crore, part of the anchor book is reserved for domestic mutual funds, and anchors never pay less than the final issue price; if that price ends up higher, they pay the difference. Their shares are locked in: half for 30 days and the rest for 90 days after allotment. A strong anchor book, announced the evening before opening, often sets the tone for subscription. Hong Kong and other markets use cornerstone investors, who commit earlier and accept longer lock-ups. Do not read anchor demand as a guarantee: anchors can sell once their lock-in ends.
example: Say ABC Ltd's ₹1,000 crore IPO reserves 50% for QIBs, or ₹500 crore. Up to 60% of that, ₹300 crore, can go to anchor investors the day before the issue opens, and half of each anchor's shares stay locked for 30 days and the other half for 90 days.

short: The first detailed offer document a company files with the market regulator before an IPO, describing its business, finances and risks, without the final price.
kid: Before opening a lemonade stand to the whole street, you write a booklet about your stand and show it to a grown-up checker. The checker asks questions before you can open.
detail: The DRHP is the preliminary offer document filed with SEBI and the stock exchanges when a company wants to go public. Prepared by the book running lead managers and lawyers, it covers the business, industry, audited financials, risk factors, litigation, promoters, the objects of the issue and the planned split between fresh issue and offer for sale. It is made public for comments, and SEBI may ask for changes before issuing its observations. Under the rules as of 2025, the company must then open its IPO within 12 months of those observations or file afresh. The DRHP leaves out the price band and final share numbers, which come later. Analysts and journalists read it closely because it is often the first full look at a private company's numbers. Do not treat a DRHP filing as a guaranteed IPO; many filers withdraw or let approval lapse.
example: Say ABC Ltd files its DRHP in January proposing a ₹800 crore fresh issue and an offer for sale of 2 crore shares. SEBI issues its observations in April, so ABC has until the following April, 12 months later, to launch the IPO.
related: Securities and Exchange Board of India

short: The near-final IPO offer document, filed before the issue opens, containing everything except the final price and exact number of shares.
kid: This is the finished booklet about your lemonade stand that everyone can read before buying. It says everything, except the exact price you will ask on the day.
detail: After SEBI's observations on the DRHP, the company updates it and files a red herring prospectus with the Registrar of Companies, with copies to SEBI and the stock exchanges. The RHP contains the full disclosures investors rely on, along with the issue dates, but not the final issue price or exact number of shares, which depend on book building. The price band is announced separately, usually a few days before the issue opens. After pricing, the company files the final prospectus with the price and share count filled in. The name comes from the US, where a red warning on the cover told readers the document was incomplete and could change. For investors, the RHP's risk factors, objects of the issue and financial statements are the essential reading. Do not confuse the RHP with the DRHP, which is filed earlier, before regulatory review.
example: Say ABC Ltd files its RHP on 2 June for an IPO opening on 9 June, with a price band of ₹270 to ₹285 announced on 4 June. After the book closes it fixes the price at ₹285 and files the final prospectus showing 3.5 crore shares sold for 3.5 crore × ₹285 = ₹997.5 crore.

short: A series of meetings in which a company's managers and its bankers pitch a share or bond sale to large investors before it is priced.
kid: Before opening your lemonade stand, you visit the neighbours' houses to tell them why your lemonade is tasty, so they want to buy some.
detail: A roadshow is the marketing stage of an IPO, follow-on offer or bond issue. Senior management and the lead bankers present the investment case to fund managers in one-on-one and group meetings across financial centres such as Mumbai, Singapore, London and New York, increasingly also by video. Investors probe strategy, numbers and risks, and their feedback helps the bankers set the price band and build the book. Before a deal, pre-marketing or early-look meetings test interest without taking orders. Companies also hold non-deal roadshows, meeting investors with nothing on offer, simply to keep shareholders informed. Everything said must match the offer document, because selectively disclosing material information breaks securities law. Do not confuse an investor roadshow with a political roadshow; in Indian headlines both use the same word.
example: Say ABC Ltd's CEO and CFO hold 60 investor meetings over 8 days before a ₹2,000 crore IPO. If funds met on the roadshow then bid for ₹3,500 crore against the ₹1,000 crore institutional portion, the book is 3.5 times covered and the bankers can price at the top of the band.

short: The time around an IPO when the company and its bankers must limit public promotion and research, so investors rely on the offer document.
kid: Before the big lemonade sale, you are not allowed to shout extra boasts about your lemonade. Everyone reads the same honest sign and decides for themselves.
detail: A quiet period restricts what an issuer and its underwriters may say publicly while a share sale is being prepared and just after it lists. The aim is to stop hype outside the official offer document, where every claim is reviewed and carries legal liability. In the US, SEC 'gun-jumping' rules limit publicity before and during an offering, and FINRA rules as of 2025 bar underwriting banks from publishing research until 10 days after an IPO; the burst of analyst coverage that follows marks the quiet-period expiry. India's SEBI rules likewise require IPO advertisements and publicity to be consistent with the offer document. A second, informal meaning confuses many students: the weeks before quarterly results when listed companies avoid talking to analysts, better called an earnings blackout or silent period.
example: Say ABC Inc. lists on 1 March. Under a 10-day research quiet period, its underwriting banks can publish their first analyst reports on 11 March, and the stock often moves that day as several ratings appear at once.

short: The investment bank that manages a share offer: preparing documents, dealing with the regulator, marketing to investors, building the order book and setting the price.
kid: When you open a big lemonade stand, a grown-up helper writes the signs, tells the neighbours about it, counts how many cups people want, and helps you pick the price.
detail: A book running lead manager is the merchant bank that runs a book-built issue. In India BRLMs must be SEBI-registered merchant bankers, and their work spans due diligence on the company, drafting the DRHP and RHP, answering SEBI's queries, lining up anchor investors, running the roadshow, managing the bid book, recommending the final price with the company and coordinating allotment and listing. Large IPOs appoint several BRLMs, often a mix of Indian and global banks, who split the fees and league table credit. Globally the equivalent is the bookrunner or lead underwriter, and the 'lead left' bank named first on the cover usually does the most work. BRLMs share responsibility for the accuracy of disclosures, which is why their due diligence matters. Do not confuse them with the registrar to the issue, which processes applications and allotment, or with syndicate members who only collect bids.
example: Say ABC Ltd appoints four BRLMs for a ₹2,000 crore IPO and agrees total fees of 2% of the issue size. The fee pool is ₹2,000 crore × 2% = ₹40 crore, or ₹10 crore per bank if split equally.

short: When a bank guarantees a share or bond sale by agreeing to buy any securities investors do not take, earning a fee for the risk.
kid: You bake 100 cookies to sell. A grown-up promises: any cookies nobody buys, I will buy myself. For that promise, you give the grown-up a few cookies.
detail: Underwriting in capital markets means a bank, or a group of banks called a syndicate, takes on the risk of a securities issue. In a firm commitment deal, the underwriter buys the whole issue from the company at a set price and resells it to investors, keeping the difference, called the gross spread, and bearing any loss if demand is weak. In a best efforts deal, the bank only promises to try to sell and takes no price risk. In India, book-built IPOs are formally underwritten only after pricing, once the book is known, so underwriters usually carry little real risk; if the fresh issue does not reach 90% subscription, the money is refunded under SEBI rules as of 2025. Do not confuse this with insurance underwriting, which means judging and pricing insurance risks, or loan underwriting, which means assessing a borrower.
example: Say a bank agrees to buy 1 crore shares from ABC Ltd at ₹95 and resell them at ₹100, a gross spread of ₹5 per share or ₹5 crore in total. If demand is weak and it can sell only at ₹92, it loses ₹3 per share, or ₹3 crore, instead.
formula: Gross spread = Offer price − Price paid to the issuer

short: A clause letting bankers sell up to 15% extra shares in an offer and use them to steady the price after listing.
kid: You borrow a few extra cookies from a friend to sell. If cookie prices drop, you buy cookies back cheaply to return them. If prices go up, you bake new ones to repay your friend.
detail: A greenshoe or over-allotment option lets the underwriters, acting through a stabilising agent, sell more shares than the base offer, usually up to 15% more, by borrowing them from promoters or existing holders. This leaves the syndicate short. If the share price falls below the issue price after listing, the agent buys shares in the market to close the short, and that buying supports the price. If the price rises, the agent instead exercises the option to buy new shares from the company at the issue price, so the company raises more money. Either way the bank is protected. The name comes from the Green Shoe Manufacturing Company, whose 1960s offering first used it. SEBI's ICDR Regulations permit it, but it is rarely used in Indian IPOs. Do not mistake stabilisation for market manipulation: it is disclosed, time-limited and legal.
example: Say ABC Ltd's base IPO is 10 crore shares at ₹100 and the bankers over-allot 1.5 crore more, or 15%. If the price falls to ₹90, the agent buys 1.5 crore shares in the market for ₹135 crore to return the borrowed shares; if it rises to ₹120, the agent exercises the option and ABC issues 1.5 crore new shares at ₹100, raising an extra ₹150 crore.
formula: Greenshoe shares = Base offer size × Over-allotment percentage (typically up to 15%)

short: When investors apply for more shares than are on offer in an IPO or other issue, measured as how many times demand exceeds supply.
kid: You have 10 cookies, but 30 friends ask for one. More friends want cookies than you have, so not everyone gets one.
detail: An issue is oversubscribed when bids exceed the shares offered. Dividing shares bid for by shares on offer gives the 'times subscribed' figure, reported for each investor category, such as QIBs, non-institutional investors and retail in Indian IPOs, and for the issue overall, usually excluding the anchor portion. Strong subscription lets the issuer price at the top of the band and signals demand, but it also means most applicants get few or no shares; in India, an oversubscribed retail book is allotted by lottery, one minimum lot per winning applicant. Undersubscription is the opposite: if a fresh issue fails to reach 90% subscription under SEBI rules as of 2025, the money is refunded. Do not read huge subscription numbers as a promise of listing gains, since part of the demand can be leveraged or speculative bidding.
example: Say ABC Ltd's retail portion offers 35 lakh shares and receives bids for 1.4 crore shares. That is 1.4 crore / 35 lakh = 4 times subscribed, so if every applicant bid for one lot, roughly one in four would get an allotment.
formula: Subscription (times) = Shares bid for / Shares offered

short: A set time after a share sale during which certain shareholders, such as promoters or anchor investors, are not allowed to sell their shares.
kid: After the lemonade stand opens to the street, the family who started it promises not to sell their pieces for a while, so the street knows they are staying.
detail: A lock-in, called a lock-up abroad, stops certain holders from selling shares for a fixed time after an IPO or other issue, so insiders cannot cash out the moment the stock lists. In India SEBI sets the lock-ins; under the rules as of 2025, the promoters' minimum contribution of 20% of post-issue capital is locked for 18 months and any extra promoter holding for 6 months (3 years and 1 year if the issue funds capital expenditure), most pre-IPO investors' shares for 6 months, and anchor investors' shares for 30 days on half and 90 days on the rest. US lock-ups are contracts with the underwriters, typically for 180 days. When a lock-in ends, a large block of shares becomes free to sell, so prices often weaken around expiry dates. Do not confuse this with the lock-in of ELSS mutual funds or tax-saving deposits, which is a different rule.
example: Say ABC Ltd's promoters own 60% after listing and a family office, as a pre-IPO investor, owns 10%. Under the rules as of 2025, 20 percentage points of the promoter stake are locked for 18 months and the other 40 points for 6 months, while the family office can sell only after 6 months; on that date a further 50% of the company's shares becomes free to sell, which markets watch closely.

short: The profit an IPO investor makes when a newly listed share trades above its issue price on its first day of trading.
kid: You bought a toy for 10 coins before the shop opened. On opening day, people want it so much they offer you 13 coins. Those 3 extra coins are your gain.
detail: Listing gains are the difference between an IPO's issue price and its price on the first day of trading, measured either at the opening price set in the pre-open session or at the day's close. Media reports usually quote the percentage premium over the issue price; a fall below it is a listing loss or listing at a discount. Many retail investors apply to Indian IPOs mainly for listing gains, using grey market premium chatter as a guide. Gains booked by selling within 12 months count as short-term capital gains on listed equity under the tax rules as of 2025. A big pop says as much about the pricing as about the business: it can mean the issuer priced too low. Do not confuse listing-day performance with long-term returns; plenty of stocks that soared on debut later fell below their issue price.
example: Say ABC Ltd's IPO is priced at ₹200 and the stock opens at ₹260 on listing day. The listing gain is (₹260 − ₹200) / ₹200 = 30%, and a retail investor allotted 75 shares gains 75 × ₹60 = ₹4,500 before tax and charges.
formula: Listing gain (%) = (Listing price − Issue price) / Issue price × 100

short: The tendency for IPO shares to be priced below what the market will pay, so they usually jump on the first trading day.
kid: If you sell your drawing for 5 coins, but friends would happily have paid 8, you got less than you could have. Those 3 coins stayed in their pockets.
detail: IPO underpricing describes the well-documented pattern that new issues, on average, close their first trading day above the offer price. Jay Ritter's long-running US data show average first-day returns well into double digits since 1980, and studies of Indian IPOs find similar or larger figures. Explanations include compensating uninformed investors for the winner's curse, where they get full allocations mainly in weak deals; rewarding institutions for revealing their true demand during book building; signalling quality; limiting legal liability; and bankers favouring their investor clients. For the company and selling shareholders, underpricing is a real cost, measured as money left on the table. Do not confuse underpricing with undervaluation of the business: it is about the gap between issue price and first-day price, not long-run fair value, and many underpriced IPOs go on to underperform over the following years.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells 5 crore shares at ₹100 and the stock closes its first day at ₹130. Underpricing is 30%, and the money left on the table is 5 crore × (₹130 − ₹100) = ₹150 crore that the company and selling shareholders could have raised.
formula: Money left on the table = (First-day closing price − Offer price) × Number of shares sold

short: A shell company that lists through an IPO with no business, then uses the cash raised to merge with a private company.
kid: Friends put coins in an empty box and promise to buy a good lemonade stand with them later. If they cannot find one in time, everyone gets their coins back.
detail: A SPAC, or blank-cheque company, raises money in an IPO, typically at $10 a unit in the US, and holds the cash in a trust while its sponsors search for a private company to acquire, usually within 18 to 24 months. The merger, called the de-SPAC, takes the target public without a traditional IPO. Before it closes, SPAC shareholders vote and may redeem their shares for their slice of the trust, so a deal can lose much of its cash. Sponsors typically receive a promote of about 20% of the shares for a nominal sum, which can dilute other investors heavily. SPACs boomed in 2020 and 2021, then faded after poor returns and tighter SEC rules adopted in 2024. Under the rules as of 2025, Indian exchanges do not allow SPAC listings, though GIFT City's IFSC framework does, and ReNew Power listed on Nasdaq in 2021 through a SPAC merger.
example: Say a SPAC sells 20 million units at $10, putting $200 million in trust, and its sponsor holds 5 million founder shares, or 5 / 25 = 20% of the total. If holders of 70% of the public shares redeem before the de-SPAC, only $60 million of the trust is left for the merger.

short: Listing a company's existing shares on a stock exchange without a traditional underwritten IPO, so the price is set by trading on day one.
kid: Instead of a grown-up helper setting the price of your toys, you put them on the shelf at the market and let buyers and sellers decide the price that morning.
detail: In a direct listing, a company's existing shares start trading on an exchange without underwriters buying and reselling a block of new shares. There is no book building or price band; the exchange runs an opening auction, guided by a reference price, and the first trade sets the market value. Spotify used the route on the NYSE in 2018 and Coinbase on Nasdaq in 2021. The appeal is lower fees, no IPO discount and no dilution, but the classic version raises no new money and the price can swing without stabilisation. Since 2020 US exchanges also allow primary direct listings that sell new shares in the opening auction. In India the phrase also describes the 2024 framework letting Indian companies list directly on GIFT City's IFSC exchanges, a different idea. A direct public offering, where a firm sells shares to investors without banks, is related but distinct.
example: Say XYZ Inc. has 100 million existing shares and lists directly with no new shares. If the opening auction clears at $40, the company is valued at 100 million × $40 = $4 billion, yet it raises no cash and pays no underwriting spread.

short: A single large sale or purchase of a listed company's shares, privately arranged with institutions and usually priced at a small discount to the market.
kid: Instead of selling toy cars one at a time at the fair, you sell a whole box of them to one big buyer in one go, for a slightly lower price each.
detail: A block trade moves a large parcel of a listed company's shares, often a promoter, private equity or strategic stake, in one negotiated transaction rather than many small orders that would push the price down. An investment bank finds buyers among institutions, usually a few percent below the last close. In a bought deal, the bank buys the whole block from the seller at a fixed price and then resells it, taking the price risk in return for the spread; in an accelerated bookbuild, the bank gathers orders first. In India, large negotiated blocks go through the exchanges' block deal window or the normal market, where, under the rules as of 2025, trades above 0.5% of a company's shares are reported as bulk deals. Block sales can weigh on a share briefly because of the discount and extra supply, but strong institutional take-up can also reassure the market.
example: Say a promoter sells 2 crore shares of ABC Ltd at ₹475, a 5% discount to the ₹500 close, raising ₹950 crore. In a bought deal, if the bank paid ₹475 and resells at ₹485 it earns ₹20 crore, but if it can only resell at ₹465 it loses ₹20 crore.
formula: Block discount = (Last close − Block price) / Last close

short: A quick share sale in which bankers collect institutional orders overnight, then price and allocate a large block of shares at a discount.
kid: You want to share out a big box of marbles quickly. Tonight you phone all the marble collectors, ask how many they want, and by morning the box is shared out.
detail: An accelerated bookbuild is a compressed offering of shares in an already listed company, used when a shareholder wants to sell a large stake, or the company wants to raise equity, with minimal market exposure. The bank launches the deal after the market closes, sounds out institutional investors by phone, builds an order book over a few hours and prices it before the next morning's open, typically at a discount of a few percent to the last close. Unlike a bought deal, the bank does not usually buy the shares upfront, though it may guarantee a minimum price through a backstop. Speed limits the risk of the price falling while news leaks. In India, ABB-style sales are commonly executed through the block deal window, the OFS mechanism or a QIP. Do not confuse an ABB with a fully marketed follow-on offering, which involves days of roadshows and retail participation.
example: Say a private equity fund decides after the close to sell 3 crore shares of ABC Ltd, which ended the day at ₹1,000. By midnight the book is covered at ₹950, a 5% discount, and the fund receives 3 crore × ₹950 = ₹2,850 crore before fees.
formula: ABB discount = (Last close − Placement price) / Last close

short: The part of an investment bank that helps companies and shareholders raise money or sell stakes through shares, such as IPOs, QIPs and block trades.
kid: Some helpers are experts at finding people who want to own pieces of a lemonade stand. When a stand needs coins, these helpers find the buyers.
detail: Equity capital markets refers both to the market for raising money through shares and to the investment-bank team that originates and executes those deals. An ECM desk advises on IPOs, follow-on offers, QIPs, rights issues, offers for sale, block trades, accelerated bookbuilds and equity-linked securities such as convertible bonds. It sits between the industry coverage bankers who own client relationships and the syndicate and sales teams who talk to investors, and it judges market windows, valuation, structure, pricing and allocation. ECM revenue is cyclical: fees surge in rising markets and dry up in sell-offs. India has become one of the world's busiest ECM markets, with record equity fundraising in 2024. Do not confuse ECM with equity research or equity sales and trading, which analyse and trade shares after issuance rather than create them.
example: Say a bank's ECM desk earns 2% on a ₹2,000 crore IPO and 1% on a ₹1,500 crore QIP in a quarter. Its fees are ₹40 crore + ₹15 crore = ₹55 crore, before sharing with any co-managers.

short: The part of an investment bank that helps governments and companies borrow by issuing bonds, debentures and other debt to investors.
kid: When a lemonade stand wants to borrow coins and promise to pay them back with a little extra, these helpers find the friends willing to lend.
detail: Debt capital markets covers the issuance of bonds and similar securities and the investment-bank team that arranges it. A DCM desk advises borrowers such as companies, banks, NBFCs, state governments and sovereigns on timing, tenor, structure, currency and pricing, then markets the issue to investors and builds the order book. Pricing is usually set as a spread over a benchmark, such as the government bond yield of similar maturity, and reflects the issuer's credit rating. Products include corporate bonds and debentures, commercial paper, green and sustainability bonds, masala bonds and dollar bonds sold abroad. In India most corporate bonds are privately placed with institutions through the exchanges' electronic bidding platforms. DCM work is steadier than ECM because companies refinance debt in most market conditions. Do not confuse DCM with fixed income trading, which buys and sells bonds after they are issued.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues ₹1,000 crore of 5-year bonds at a coupon of 8.10% when, say, the 5-year government bond yields 6.60%. The spread is 1.50 percentage points (150 basis points), and ABC pays ₹1,000 crore × 8.10% = ₹81 crore of interest a year.
formula: Issue yield = Benchmark government bond yield + Credit spread

short: Rankings of investment banks and advisers by the value, number or fees of deals they worked on over a period.
kid: It is like a sticker chart in class showing which helper helped the most friends this term. The helper at the top gets to show it off.
detail: League tables rank banks, law firms and other advisers by their share of deals in a period, such as M&A advisory, equity offerings or bond issues in a calendar year. Data providers such as LSEG, Dealogic, Bloomberg and Mergermarket compile them, along with Indian trackers such as Prime Database for public issues. Rankings can be by deal value, number of deals or estimated fees, and each provider has its own crediting rules; in a typical equity offering, the issue value is split equally among the bookrunners. Banks chase league table positions because clients treat them as a signal of experience when awarding mandates, so pitch books often open with them. Read them with care: one mega-deal can lift a bank many places, rankings differ by provider and criteria, and a high spot by value does not mean a bank earned the most fees or did the best work.
example: Say a ₹3,000 crore IPO has six bookrunners, so each gets ₹3,000 crore / 6 = ₹500 crore of league table credit. A bank that also ran a ₹800 crore QIP alone ends the year with ₹500 crore + ₹800 crore = ₹1,300 crore of ECM credit.
formula: League table credit per bookrunner = Deal value / Number of bookrunners

short: New shares a company creates and sells in an offering, so the money raised goes to the company itself rather than existing shareholders.
kid: You make brand-new pieces of your lemonade stand and sell them. The coins go into the stand's own piggy bank to buy more lemons.
detail: A fresh issue is the primary part of an offering in which the company issues new shares and keeps the proceeds, adding to both its share count and its cash. It contrasts with an offer for sale, where existing holders sell their shares and keep the money. Indian IPOs often combine both, and the split matters: a large fresh issue funds growth, debt repayment or capital expenditure, while a pure offer for sale mainly lets promoters and funds exit. SEBI rules as of 2025 require the offer document to spell out the objects of the fresh issue, cap money kept for general corporate purposes at 25% of proceeds, and require a monitoring agency to track its use when the fresh issue exceeds ₹100 crore. Because new shares are created, existing holders are diluted. Do not assume the whole IPO size reaches the company; check the fresh issue figure.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 40 crore shares, all owned by its promoter, and sells 10 crore new shares at ₹150 in a fresh issue. The company receives 10 crore × ₹150 = ₹1,500 crore, the share count rises to 50 crore, and the promoter's stake falls from 100% to 80%.
formula: Fresh issue proceeds = New shares issued × Issue price

short: A deal in which investors buy new shares directly from an already listed company in a private, negotiated sale, usually at a discount.
kid: Your lemonade stand is already open to the street. A neighbour quietly offers to buy a few new pieces straight from you for a little less, and you get coins quickly.
detail: A PIPE, or private investment in public equity, is a sale of newly issued shares or convertible securities by a listed company directly to selected investors, such as hedge funds, private equity funds or strategic partners. Terms are negotiated privately, usually at a discount to the market price, and the deal can close in days without a public offering. Companies use PIPEs when they need capital fast, when markets are volatile, or when a public offer would be too costly or slow. PIPEs became familiar as part of SPAC mergers, where investors commit extra cash alongside the trust. Because new shares are issued, existing holders are diluted, and a deep discount can signal distress. In India the closest equivalent is a preferential allotment, which must follow SEBI's pricing floor, shareholder approval and lock-in rules. Do not confuse a PIPE with a private placement by an unlisted company.
example: Say XYZ Inc. trades at $20 and sells 5 million new shares to three funds at $18, a 10% discount. It raises 5 million × $18 = $90 million within a week, and a holder of 1 million of the existing 45 million shares sees their stake fall from about 2.22% to 2.00%.
formula: PIPE discount = (Market price − PIPE price) / Market price

short: Selling shares or bonds directly to a small, chosen group of investors instead of offering them to the general public.
kid: Instead of selling your cookies to everyone at the fair, you quietly offer them to a few friends you choose. It is faster and needs fewer signs.
detail: A private placement is an offer of securities to a limited set of identified investors, such as banks, mutual funds, insurers, family offices or wealthy individuals, rather than to the public. Because the buyers are fewer and more sophisticated, disclosure is lighter and the deal is faster and cheaper than a public issue. In India, section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs it: under the rules as of 2025, an offer may go to at most 200 persons in a financial year, excluding qualified institutional buyers and employees under stock option schemes, through a private placement offer letter, with money received only through banking channels. Private placement dominates the Indian corporate bond market, where most debentures are placed with institutions and then listed. QIPs and preferential allotments are specific kinds of private placement by listed companies with their own SEBI rules; do not treat the terms as interchangeable.
example: Say ABC Ltd raises ₹300 crore by privately placing 3-year debentures with five institutions, each taking ₹60 crore at a 9% coupon. It pays ₹300 crore × 9% = ₹27 crore of interest a year and avoids the time and cost of a public bond issue.

short: The work of combining two companies' people, systems and operations after a merger, so the deal delivers its promised benefits.
kid: Two friends join their lemonade stands into one. Now they must decide whose jug to use, who pours and who collects coins, so the new stand works smoothly.
detail: Post-merger integration covers everything that happens after a deal closes to turn two organisations into one: leadership and reporting lines, people and pay, IT and finance systems, supply chains, branding, customers and culture. It is usually run by an integration management office with a 100-day plan and tracked against the synergies promised to shareholders, such as cost savings from shared functions or extra revenue from cross-selling. Studies regularly find that many acquisitions fail to create value, and poor integration, such as clashing cultures, lost talent or broken systems, is a leading reason. In India, Air India's absorption of Vistara in November 2024 meant merging fleets, crews, loyalty programmes and booking systems. Integration also brings one-off costs that can weigh on profits for a year or two. Do not confuse integration with due diligence, which happens before signing. PMI here is unrelated to the purchasing managers' index.
example: Say XYZ Ltd buys ABC Ltd promising ₹500 crore of annual cost synergies by year three, at a one-off integration cost of ₹600 crore. If year-one savings are ₹200 crore, the team has delivered 40% of the target and recovered a third of the integration cost.

short: A secure online folder where a seller shares confidential documents with potential buyers or investors so they can check the business before a deal.
kid: Before swapping your toy box with a friend, you let them look inside a special locked box with all your toys and notes, so they know exactly what they are getting.
detail: A data room holds the documents bidders need for due diligence: audited and management accounts, tax filings, customer and supplier contracts, loans, licences, property papers, litigation, employee terms and intellectual property. Once physical rooms in lawyers' offices, they are now virtual data rooms on secure platforms with permission levels, watermarking, download controls, a question-and-answer module and logs of who viewed what. The sell-side bankers and lawyers decide which bidders see which folders, often releasing the most sensitive material only to final bidders, sometimes through a 'clean team' when the buyer is a competitor. Data rooms are also used in IPO due diligence, fund-raising and sales of stressed assets under India's insolvency process. Bidders sign a non-disclosure agreement before access. Do not confuse the data room with the information memorandum, the marketing summary sent earlier to attract interest.
example: Say the seller of ABC Ltd uploads 4,000 documents and admits five bidders for six weeks. Access logs show Bidder C opened 3,200 documents, or 80%, while Bidder E opened only 400, or 10%, a useful hint to the banker about who is serious.

short: A way for a company planning an IPO to file its draft offer document with the regulator privately, making it public only after review.
kid: You show your lemonade stand plan only to the grown-up checker first, in secret. If you change your mind, nobody on the street even knows you thought about it.
detail: SEBI introduced the confidential pre-filing route in late 2022 as an alternative to the normal public DRHP. The company files a pre-filed draft offer document that SEBI and the exchanges review but do not publish. After SEBI's observations, the company files an updated draft, UDRHP-I, which is made public for 21 days of comments, and then an RHP. Under the rules as of 2025, the IPO must open within 18 months of SEBI's final observations, longer than the 12 months allowed on the normal route. The main benefit is privacy: sensitive numbers stay away from competitors, and a company can drop or delay its IPO without a public withdrawal. Tata Play was among the first users, and Swiggy used the route before its 2024 IPO. The US SEC offers a similar confidential draft submission. Do not assume the route skips disclosure: everything becomes public before the offer opens.
example: Say ABC Ltd pre-files confidentially in January and receives SEBI's final observations in June. It then has 18 months, until December of the following year, to open its IPO, and if markets sour it can let the window lapse without a public withdrawal.
related: Securities and Exchange Board of India
